187709:
Letter in Support of LD 581 "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program"
Submitted by Amy Eckland
Dear Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Education and
Cultural Affairs Committee,
As a student of the Maine Track Program, I am writing to support LD 581, "An Act to
Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program." I grew up in Kennebunk, Maine where I attended the local public schools. I didn't realize I wanted to be a doctor until I was an undergraduate, but even before then, I had heard about the Maine Track and related scholarships. Medical school felt so much more achievable knowing those opportunities existed for students
like me. I ultimately decided to pursue a career in medicine due to my interest in both science and the humanities, and my desire to work in a field where I could collaborate with others to
solve problems with a direct impact on individuals and communities.
As I considered careers in medicine, I knew becoming a physician was the best path for
my goals, but the cost presented a significant barrier. I would need to take out loans to cover the cost of medical school as well as living expenses for four years on top of my existing
undergraduate loans. Furthermore, as a Maine resident, I did not have any programs available to
me with in-state tuition rates. I estimated that I was likely to graduate with up to $400 thousand in debt without assistance. This intimidating figure nearly convinced me to pursue a different career, but I ultimately decided medical school was the right path for me despite the cost.
I loved my Maine Track interview. I knew I would fit in at this program and get an excellent education in line with my values. I was also excited at the possibility of learning medicine in the community that raised me and where I was already a member of the health care workforce in my gap year. However, my decision would ultimately have to come down to cost. When I received my financial aid offers that spring, I needed to choose the program that would leave me with the least debt. It was only because of the Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship
that this program was the Tufts Maine Track.
Without my scholarship, I would have selected an out-of-state program to pursue my medical and public health education. I am so grateful for the funding that allowed me to enroll at the school that was the best fit for me and my goals. The mentors and peers I have met here have defined my training so far and will continue to influence me going forward. While I will be
attending a residency program elsewhere, I look forward to ultimately returning to Maine later in
my career. My time as a trainee at Maine Medical Center is a major factor in my desire to do so.
If we lose funding for some of these scholarships, I believe we will also lose future students like
myself with the potential to become physicians for Maine communities.

Thank you, Amy Eckland TUSM-MMC MD/MPH Candidate, 2025
187710:
Letter of Support for LD 581
An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program
March 31, 2025
Dear Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education,
My name is Annika Gallandt, I am a third~year medical student at the Tufts University Maine
Track Program, a recipient of the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship, and I am writing in
support of LD 581. I was born and raised in central Maine and for my entire life being a `Mainer 9 has been at the core of my identity. Although I left my home state for college, I always knew that
I would return to settle in Maine, this is where I want to work, contribute to community, and
eventually raise a family of my own.
Growing up I witnessed how many Mainers have difficulties accessing care due to geographic and financial barriers. Part of what drew me to pursue a career as a physician was the unique
ability to treat and advocate for individual patients while also improving access to healthcare for entire communities. However, as I started to research medical school programs it became clear to
me that the financial burden of medical school tuition would likely dictate both where I went to
school and possibly the medical specialty I would eventually choose. The freedom to return to
my home state to practice in a rural area felt at odds with the immense financial burden of medical school tuition and the student loans I would accumulate. When I learned that the Tufts
Maine Track program offered scholarships to qualified students to make the cost of attendance
comparable to in-state tuition I knew this was the program that was most in-line with my
personal and professional goals.
The Maine Track is comprised of highly successful students all of whom chose this program for
its exemplary academics as well as its dedication to community-based medicine. I along with the
majority of my classmates were accepted into multiple medical schools and had a choice when it
came to selecting what program to attend. My decision and the decision of many of my peers
was strongly influenced by the financial support offered by the Doctors for Maine's Future
Scholarship Program. Receiving scholarship support made my decision to commit to the Maine Track easy. In my three years as a student in the program the financial support from this scholarship has given me freedom to explore and consider careers in all fields of medicine. It has
removed much of the financial pressure to choose a specialized career based on future compensation and rather has given me the opportunity to weigh personal interests, community
need, and ability to practice at a rural hospital into my decision.
The Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship doesn't solely impact student recipients, it also
indirectly influences healthcare provided to Maine citizens. In my clinical rotations I have seen
firsthand the enthusiasm and support Mainers have for the Maine Track program and its potential
to improve the urgent need for physicians in rural communities. 74% of former Maine Track students who completed their residencies in Maine stay in state to practice. From my own experience and the experiences of my classmates, training in Maine for medical school has
increased our interest in staying here for residency. Put simply, Maine's investment in medical

students has already impacted the physician workforce across the state in a positive way. Terminating funding for the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program will have widespread negative impacts both for future medical students and patients across the state of
Maine. I urge you to support LD 581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future
Scholarship Program" to support the future of medical education in Maine and the health of all Maine citizens and communities.
Sincerely,
Annika Mallory Gallandt Tufts University School of Medicine -- Maine Track Program Class of 2026

While many recognize the high cost of medical education, it may not be as common knowledge that many expenses begin well before an acceptance letter. In addition to costs incurred from a 4-year
undergraduate degree and prerequisite coursework, standard registration for the Medical College
Admissions Test (MCAT), a notoriously important requirement for medical school applications, costs
$345. Should a student need to retake this exam (i.e. to try for a more competitive score) they will need to pay this amount again. If they need to cancel or reschedule, they will have to pay anwvhere from $50$2O0 without a full refund. Given the high stakes of this exam, many students spend hundreds to even thousands of dollars on study materials or prep courses. Then come applications. The initial cost of
applying to one MD program is $175 and $198 for one DO program, plus $47 for each additional MD
program to which a student applies and $57 for each additional DO program. Furthermore, most
programs charge a fee for their secondary applications that can vary from $50-$200 each. Given that pre-medical students apply to an average of 16 programs in hopes of an interview invite, you can see
how this entire process quickly becomes a financial burden even before that first tuition bill.

So where does this leave the average medical student hopeful? Especially ones from Maine where the average individual income in 2023 was $38,152; nearly half the national average. Where does that leave
a mother of 3 from Old Town, Maine who dreams of being a doctor? Right in front of you I'm happy to say, and that is because of this scholarship. What was once an insurmountable financial hurdle, became feasible for me and my family. Because of this scholarship, I have been able to complete the entirety of my medical school training in Maine. This allowed for me to network and form great mentorships with Maine providers very early on, which undoubtedly played a role in my Match Day success on March 21" . I am thrilled to share that I get to stay in Maine for residency as part of Maine Medical Center's rural
track program in psychiatry.

Continuing to fund the Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship program is so much more than helping people pay for medical school. It gives hope to our people by addressing the significant need for doctors in Maine, and sends the message to aspiring Maine physicians that socioeconomic status should not be
what stands in the way of pursuing your dreams. Thank you to the State of Maine for investing in me and my dream, and I look forward to spending my career caring for you in return.

Bethany Miles, RN, BSN, OMS-IV Gorham, Maine

187712:
Senator Raferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Education and
Cultural Affairs Committee, as a graduate of the Maine Track Program I am writing to
support LD 581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program."
My name is Charu Tiwari, and I am from Falmouth, Maine. I ventured out of Maine to Ohio for my undergraduate education, but I wanted to return home for medical school to be closer to my family. Like many aspiring medical students, one of my considerations when
researching medical schools was tuition and the availability of scholarships. As someone who is committed to a career in primary care--one of the lowest-paid specialties--I was particularly concerned about the amount of debt I would incur during school. The financial burden of student loans is a heavy reality for many, and for me, it was an important factor in my decision-making process. I was incredibly fortunate to receive a scholarship that not
only allowed me to pursue medical school in my home state, but also made the ability to
pursue primary care a more realistic option. Opportunities liI<e this scholarship not only ease the financial strain of medical education but also empower students to choose the specialties that truly align with their passions and values.
The cost of medical education extends beyond tuition. Medical students face living expenses and the cost of board materials, often without an income. |'m sure that it is no surprise that medical school is incredibly demanding--being unable to take care of oneself physically and mentally due to financial strain on top of that does not lend itself to
academic success. Scholarships like the one I received do more than make medical
school accessible--they help to ensure that students can thrive throughout their education, maintain their well-being, and ultimately succeed in their careers.
Financial support for medical students does notjust benefit the student themselves, but it
promotes the success of the entire healthcare system. As someone who is invested in
Maine's future, I see the direct impact of financial assistance for students on the state's
healthcare needs. During my internship as an internal medicine resident physician at Maine Medical Center over the past nine months, I have frequently heard patients say how
difficult it has been for them or their loved ones to find a doctor--whether that is a primaiy
care doctor or a specialist. It is clear from my experience that Maine's healthcare system is
struggling to meet the demands of its population, especially in rural areas. We are in
desperate need of more physicians to serve these communities.
One aspect of patient care I have learned about during my training is the value of trust between patient and physician. When a patient and physician share a background or come from the same community, a unique and trusting bond is formed that improves the quality of care. By allowing Mainers to obtain a medical education in their home state, we can help cultivate a generation of doctors who are truly and deeply invested in the well-being of their
communities. Helping students address the burden of overwhelming debt accrued during medical education is a critical aspect of fostering such a community and addressing the state's healthcare challenges, particularly in rural and underserved areas.

The rising cost of living in Maine only adds to the financial pressure on medical students. Helping aspiring physicians have the financial resources to pursue education and training in Maine and eventually return to their communities will promote a sustainable healthcare workforce in the state. Financial support like this scholarship is a critical aspect of helping these students and Maine's healthcare system achieve their goals.
Though I still have a couple years of residency ahead of me, my hope is to remain in Maine and continue to serve its people. This state is my home, and I am committed to giving back
to the community that shaped me. I support LD 581 because I believe it will further enhance Maine's healthcare system, creating a healthier, more sustainable future for all
its residents. By ensuring that students can pursue their medical education here, we are
making a powerful investment in the future of Maine and its people.

Testimony of Dena Whitesell, MD
MaineHealth/Tufts University School of Medicine
In Support of LD 581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future
Scholarship Program" March 31, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of the Education and
Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Dena Whitesell, MD, Assistant Dean for Students for the Tufts University School of Medicine and Attending Psychiatrist for MaineHealth, and I am here to testify in strong support of LD 581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship
Program."
MaineHealth is an integrated non-profit health care system that provides the full continuum of
health care services to the residents of eleven counties in Maine and one in New Hampshire.
MaineHealth is also the state's largest private employer with over 24,000 care team members,
but we are facing a workforce crisis that is significantly impacting access to care, and are
currently recruiting for 117 physicians.
Though I am "from away" I am very familiar with the barriers that people face seeking . healthcare in rural areas. I grew up on my uncle's farm in upstate New York over an hour's drive from the nearest hospital. As the first person in my family to attend college, much less attain a graduate degree, I am also acutely aware of the struggles that students face when seeking
higher education but facing hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt.
Maine Medical Center (MMC) partnered with the Tufts University School of Medicine (TUSM)
in 2008 to start an allopathic medical school program designed to address the shortage of physicians in Maine, particularly in our rural areas, and to give Maine student's access to highquality medical education at a tuition cost similar to that of a state-sponsored program. The unique Maine Track program offers a rigorous training program that exposes students to rural clinical practice from day one and provides students firsthand experience providing care in local communities throughout the state including such towns as Madison, Caribou, Belfast, Wiscasset, Richmond, and Norway.
Maine Medical Center also guarantees that at least 20 Maine students in each class receive scholarships of $25,000 per year, totaling more than $2 million each year. The scholarships have been raised through the generosity of private donors, local companies, and, very importantly, the Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship program, which was created by the 124th Maine Legislature and administered by the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME). The Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship program is a public-private partnership between the State and Tufts --
Maine Track and the University of New England College of Osteopathic Medicine, as each
school is required to match the state-funded scholarships, l:l.
As I shared during your Biennial Budget hearings, the proposed funding for the Doctors for
Maine's Future scholarship program in the FAME section of the Biennial Budget will reduce the

number of scholarships to 3 students at each institution, and eventually 2 students at each institution. It is important to note that the reduction in scholarships also reduces the number of . scholarships required to be matched by both schools. This could result in fewer scholarships for
Maine~based students. And that is why we are incredibly grateful to Senator Bennett for bringing this bill forward, which provides the absolute minimum funding necessary to continue to the
current number of scholarships.

The Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship program l1as been very successful i11 achieving its goal of encouraging Maine students to enter medical school, and, it is clear that the Maine Track program is critically important in producing local physicians:

@ 0 74% of Maine Track students who completed their residency in Maine are practicing in

Maine. This is exceptionally high in comparison to

from the Association of

American Medical Colleges' , which found that a 58.6% of the individuals who completed

residency training from 2014 to 2023 are practicing in the state where they did their

residency training.

0 Nationally, the number of individuals applying to medical school declined by over 7% last year, but Maine saw an increase of 8% from the year prior.
0 The Maine Track Class of 2025 includes 42 students---20 of these students grew up in
Maine.

0 To date, 429 physicians over 11 classes have graduated from the Mai11e Track Program.
278 were from Maine.

0 The program is accessible. We are very proud to offer a Mai11e Track Early Assurance
Program for sophomores at Bates College, Bowdoin College, Colby College, and all
University of Maine campuses. Additionally, The MMC-TUSM acceptance rate last year
for Mainers into the Maine Track was 47%. For those from away, our acceptance rate
was only 17%. This compares very favorably to TUSM's overall acceptance rate of approximately 4% and the average national acceptance rate of approximately 5.5%.
0 The Maine Track program has come full circle. Graduates are now faculty teaching current students. Caleb Swanberg, MD, class of 2015, who has spoken to you in the past, precepts students in Family Medicine when they rotate in Caribou for nine months. The site director for our rural site in Norway is a former graduate. Another graduate from the
class of 2023 is a second year resident in the newly formed Rural Track of the Psychiatry Residency program at Maine Medical Center. There are countless other examples.
One significant challenge we face in retaining our medical school graduates, however, is that
states' residency slots have been limited by funding to support graduate medical education from the Federal government. MaineHealth l1as been able to increase the number of resident and
fellowship positions through our own resources, recognizing this as a solution to our physician
workforce needs. But more needs to be done to ensure that Maine-trained students have access to a residency placements in Maine. Recent reports show that Maine is the 8"` best state at retaining

physicians who complete their residency in Maine. We can further enhance the effectiveness of
the Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship program if we can increase the number of residency
slots in Maine.
As the Legislature seeks to increase access to health care, including behavioral health care, it is critical that investments be made in increasing the pipeline of future health care workers, like the Doctors for Maine's Future scholarship program.
Thank you and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
187715:
Testimony of Grace Gile
in Strong Support of LD 581 "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program"
March 31, 2025
Senator Raferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and distinguished members of the Education
and Cultural Affairs Committee, as a student of the Maine Track Program I am testifying today
in strong support of LD 581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship
Program."
My name is Grace Gile, and I am a York County native where I grew up on an apple farm in
Alfred. I am a member of the class of 2026 at Tufts University School of Medicine on the Maine
Track and a current Doctors for Maine's Future Scholar. There is no doubt that this scholarship
has allowed me to receive an excellent education in my home state, without worry of substantial
financial burden.
I grew up in a family of traditions: my father is a ninth-generation farmer, my mother a thirdgeneration nurse. I always knew I wanted to follow in my mom's footsteps and work in healthcare but wanted to create my own path in my career. In college, I never even considered
medicine as a career because of the notorious financial burden of attending medical school. It felt
like something that I, the first person in my family to move away and obtain a four-year degree,
was simply unable to do. It wasn't until I had heard about the Maine Track program and the scholarships available to students from Maine that I was able to picture myself becoming a
physician.
The Maine Track is a program that not only invests in its students, but it also invests in the state of Maine. It provides the state with a vital resource: access to highly trained physicians. The program emphasizes early clinical experience throughout various communities in the state. Personally, I have been in clinics ranging from Biddeford, to Wiscasset, to Belgrade, and most
recently, I moved to Caribou for nine months and completed all my third-year rotations there.
My patients in Aroostook County knew the struggle of finding healthcare close to home: at least
twice a month a patient or their family member would beg me to come back and practice there
when I graduated. I didn't enter medical school wanting to do rural medicine, I wasn't even set
on staying in or building my career in Maine. It was my time in Caribou that showed me both the
beauty and challenges of rural medicine.
It is the unique combination of the Maine Track's curriculum and the financial support from the
Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship that have encouraged me to explore a career in rural
primary care. Without the aid that this scholarship has provided me, I would be graduating

medical school over a quarter million dollars in debt and would be much less motivated to go
through with my current career plans simply due to the burden of debt and the significantly lower
salaries in primary care specialties.
I care about this scholarship fund because I care about the community that raised me in Alfred,
the community where I assumed the role of a medical student for the first time in Wiscasset, and the community that I grew to call home in Caribou. Please vote in support of the Doctors for
Maine's Future Scholarship to not only support Mainers who dream of becoming physicians, but also to support our communities across the state who deeply need access to care.

10042809:
Letter in Support of LD 581 "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program"
Submitted by Jane Branch
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and distinguished members of Joint Standing Committee on Education, my name is Jane Branch, and I am a third-year medical student in Portland, Maine. I am writing in strong support of LD581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program"
I was raised in Orrington, Maine, a small town just outside of Bangor. Since I was a child, I wanted to be a physician. Only 6 states in this country do not have their own public medical school and Maine is one of them; so, when I left for college, I honestly didn't expect to return for my medical education. But I was fortunate enough to be accepted to the Tufts Maine Track Program, which has a class size of only 40 students each year, and that changed everything.
I am beyond grateful to be working with and learning from patients and doctors in the state of Maine. Importantly, training here has exposed me to the unique political and socioeconomic challenges our communities face. Because I train in Maine, with clinical experiences not just in Portland, but as far down east as Lubec, I have developed an intimate understanding of the health systems currently in place in Maine, and the disparities that need addressing. Because I train in Maine, I have been able to engage in conversations with physician and student colleagues regarding healthcare reform solutions for the state. Because I train in Maine, I care about the longevity of our health system, and I plan to stick around to improve it.
Medical students from private institutions like Tufts and UNECOM on average face a debt upwards of $265,000. As you might imagine, many of us are hesitant to consider a vital specialty like primary care because of these daunting financial constraints. While I am not personally a recipient, I have seen how powerful the Doctors for Maine's Futures Scholarship can be in lightening this burden.
Maine is currently facing a severe shortage of physicians. Funding for the Doctors for Maine's Futures Scholarship not only alleviates the student debt preventing doctors from entering important fields like primary care, but it also helps grow Maine's next generation of physician leaders. Now more than ever, we need them. As the Legislature seeks to improve access to health care in the state, I implore you to consider scholarships like the Doctors for Maine's Futures Scholarship essential. Supporting LD 581 and fully funding this scholarship program is a vote for restoring the health of the state.
Sincerely,
Jane Branch TUSM-MMC MD Candidate, 2026
10040180:
Tesmony from Dr. Jane Carreiro Before the Commitee on Educaon and Cultural Affairs
LD 581 An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program
Public Hearing: March 31, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representave Murphy, and disnguished members of the Educaon and Cultural Affairs Commitee, my name is Dr. Jane Carreiro, Dean of the College of Osteopathic Medicine at the University of New England. I am subming this writen tesmony on behalf of UNE, requesng that the Legislature fund the Doctors for Maine's Future program. This is an effecve program that atracts and retains physician talent to rural Maine communies. Unfortunately, no funding was dedicated to this important program in the proposed biennial budget.

Dr. Jane E. Carreiro VP Health Affairs & Dean, College of Osteopathic Medicine
10042285:
Growing up in Brewer, Maine, it was not a popular aspiration for young people to strive to become physicians. Despite being at the top of my high school class and having a strong interest in medicine, it didn't feel that attending medical school was something I could ever do. I started nursing school at eighteen years old and realized that a lot of the questions I had regarding disease were not being answered as a part of my curriculum. I began to realize that my role in the healthcare team would be better fulfilled as a physician.
Not coming from a family of physicians, I didn't understand how arduous (and expensive) this journey was about to become; however, I would certainly make the choice again. I applied to medical school and was accepted at the University of New England College of Osteopathic Medicine. The euphoria of my dreams coming to fruition and the realization that I was going to be able to train in the place I aspired to practice was abruptly diminished when I realized how much tuition for four years (plus living expenses was going to be). Like many kids I grew up with, I started part time jobs in middle school and worked all throughout college to pay my bills. The grueling sixteenhour study days and unpredictable clinical hours made it impossible to hold a job during medical school. I received a letter six weeks before day one of medical school informing me that I was a Doctor's for Maine's Future recipient.
I teared up reading that the financial hardship that had been lessened -- the scholarship I received during medical school from this fund drastically changed the amount of student debt I had to accrue. More than the money was the emotional effect it had on me. As I sat next to people with master's degrees and Ivy league educations, it made me feel the state of Maine thought I deserved to be there as well. I thought about my grandfather who travels eight hours round-trip from Madawaska to Bangor to see his cardiologist. I thought about patients who I worked with who were unable to see a specialist because the only one in the area didn't take MaineCare.
This scholarship allowed me to experience the different niches of medicine openly without the intense pressure to go into the highest paying fields because I was not graduating with nearly as much student debt as I would have without the support of DFMF. This scholarship truly altered my career trajectory. I am an Internal Medicine resident at Maine Medical Center where I hope to eventually become a hospitalist. This means I will not be pursuing any further specialization and will provide care to any adults in the state regardless of their insurance or ability to pay. I plan to practice in Maine. Without DFMF, I would feel the stress to pursue higher paying specialties or to move out of state for higher paying jobs as the student debt burden would be insurmountable. To not fund DFMF would be a great disservice to young physicians and would further exacerbate our state's significant physician shortage.

The Maine Medical Association (MMA) is a professional organization representing more than 4,000 physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine. MMA's mission is to support Maine physicians, advance the quality of medicine in Maine, and promote the health of all Maine people. The Maine Osteopathic Association (MOA) is a professional organization representing more than 1,200 osteopathic physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine whose mission is to serve the Osteopathic profession of the State of Maine through a coordinated effort of professional education, advocacy, and member services in order to ensure the availability of quality osteopathic health care to the people of this State.

Testimony of Nik Hase
In Strong Support of LD 581 "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program"
March 31, 2025
Dear Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Education, my name is Nik Hase. I am a fourth-year medical student at Tufts University who will be graduating in May and starting residency this coming June. I am here today to advocate for LD 581 which provides ongoing funds to maintain the Doctors for Maine's
Future Scholarship Program.
For me, there are two things at stake regarding this bill: the continued promotion of relationships
between Mainers, and the survival of young Maine doctors. To best illustrate these points, I want
to contrast the stories of two medical students from Maine: one is myself, and the other is my closest childhood friend. Growing up in Buxton, Maine, I first met my friend when we were 7
years old on a travel soccer team for the Bonny Eagle region, him being from Hollis, a short
drive across the Saco River from my house. Over the years, we grew close over a shared love of
philosophy, particularly a mutual belief that it is authentic relationships which bring meaning to
one's life, and decided at the end of high school that we would pursue careers in medicine as we
felt that compassion was the most forthright means to achieve genuine connection. Here our paths diverged, with him attending undergraduate school outside of the state, and myself attending the University of Maine in Orono. While there, I was fortunate enough to be accepted
into the Tufts Maine Track through their early assurance program during my sophomore year, being granted a scholarship similar to the one at stake today, while my friend was accepted into a
well-respected medical school in the northeast after completing his bachelor's degree, where he was offered no such scholarship.
Now, looking upon the dawn of residency, we each face drastically different financial obstacles, which, in his case, could make residency training in Maine financially prohibitive. What follows
is my friend's current financial situation, which, mind you, is typical of the average medical student, shared with his permission. After three years of medical school, my friend owes
$263,000 in loans, with $26,000 being left over from undergrad. He anticipates borrowing
another $85,000 to pay for tuition for his fourth year, bringing his net principle, not including
interest, to roughly $350,000, with an average interest rate of 8%. Now consider this in the
context of the current political climate: as of February of this year, income driven loan
repayment plans are no longer allowed on federal loans (which all of my friends are). Fixed payment repayment plans are all that are currently accepted at this time. Based on my friend's
principle and interest rate, his loan servicer predicts his monthly payment to be $4,200 a month on a standard fixed plan to repay his loan over 10 years.

In the context of the resident salary and cost of livi11g in the state of Maine, this monthly payment makes training in Maine for residency an impossibility. Interns in MaineHealth
residencies have an annual gross salary of $68,000. Assuming a 20% income tax, this equates to a net pay of $55,000 annually, or $4,600 a month. Given that my friend will have to pay $4,200 a
month in loans, this will leave him just $400 a month for all of his expenses, including rent and groceries, the former for which is on average $2,100 for a one bedroom apartment in Portland. Without scholarships like the one being debated today, young doctors will not only be less enticed to train and eventually practice in Maine, it will simply be a financial impossibility.
However, with this scholarship and ones similar to it, training in Maine can become a reality. In
the setting of a $100,000 scholarship, my current principal balance sits at $190,000, with $15,000 being left over from undergrad. With my interest rate, my average payment per month
will be $2,200 over 10 years. Based on this payment, I would have $2,400 left over a month on
an intern salary at MaineHealth after my loan payment, allowing me to afford the average Portland monthly rent of $2,100. This scholarship through the Maine Track Program is how we will keep young physicians in the state of Maine, 70% of whom will stay as attending and serve
their fellow Mainers in perpetuity. Without it, Mainer medical students will seek training elsewhere, not because they want to, but because they have no other choice.
My grandmother, who was a nurse at Cary Medical Center in Caribou for over 20 years, has
stressed to me about what she calls a "revolving door" of young doctors up in the County. Over
many years, she noticed that nearly every young doctor who would come to practice up in the
County would stay for three years and leave, fracturing relationships, and making it impossible for Mainers to get authentic longitudinal care. I believe that by making it possible for Mainers to
do residency in Maine, through scholarships like this one, is how we keep doctors who love this state in this state. I believe it is through scholarships like this that we stop the revolving door, and instead open a new one by which Mainers can engage in authentic longitudinal relationships with
their doctors, and build a healthier state along the way.

including on my face and neck. Every time this happened, I saw a different physician who
never seemed concerned about the number of times this had happened to me. The sixth time occurred in college, and I went to see my campus doctor. Within seconds of looking at the infection and hearing a very brief history of my recurring problem, he had a diagnosis
for me: methicillin resistant staph aureus, an increasingly common infection of normal skin bacteria that is resistant to typical antibiotics. He gave me a stronger oral antibiotic, and 3 weeks of topical antibiotic ointment to put up my nose to eliminate the resistant bacteria,
no scalpels required. I haven't had another infection since.
Now that I have 3 years of medical training under my belt, I understand that my condition is actually very easy to diagnose and treat. Perhaps if I had had a consistent provider in my

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:
My name is Bill Norbert. I am the Governmental Affairs and Communications
Manager at the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME). I am here to testify in support of L.D. 581, An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine 's Future Scholarship Program.
FAME would like to thank Senator Bennett for sponsoring this bill to provide
meaningful, ongoing funding for a program we have had the pleasure of administering
since its inception back in 2009-2010. We also wish to thank the various bipartisan co-
sponsors of the bill.
This bill would provide ongoing funding of $300,000 per year to help maintain the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program. The Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program provides a $25,000 scholarship annually for up to four years to
Maine residents attending medical school at either University of New England College of
Medicine or at Tufts University School of Medicine-Maine Medical Center Program (Maine Track Program). Schools must provide an equal number (match) of $25,000 scholarships to Maine resident students attending the school.
The Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program was created by the 124th Maine Legislature. At the time it was founded, the program scholarships were
designed to provide a tuition subsidy of fifty percent of the cost of attendance annually,
for eligible students who enter qualifying Maine-based medical school programs. This amount no longer represents fifty percent of the cost of attendance, however. The goal of
the program is to increase the number of Maine physicians and to increase the number of
physicians who practice in primary care, underserved specialties, or underserved areas of
Maine. Another goal is to increase aspirations for Maine residents, especially those with some financial need, to attend medical school in-state.

Each year FAME uses $400,000 from its overall Student Financial Assistance line
of General Fund appropriations to the program. This helps to fund four students: two awards per medical school annually, which are in turn matched by the medical schools. Over the years, the Legislature has periodically appropriated funding for the program to
help us make more than two awards per school annually. We've made three to five
awards per school traditionally depending on available funding but have had to recently reduce awards to three per school due to declining funding. This bill would help us to increase awards back to at least four per school annually.
To give you an idea of the cost/math involved: each scholarship is for $25,000 for four years of education ($100,000 per student). An additional $400,000 per year in
ongoing annual funding thus would help to fund four more students annually: two more students at each institution (which would again provide for four awards per school
annually if we count FAME's portion), and then each institution would need to match
each scholarship. After awards are made this year, there will be approximately $684,000
remaining` in program funds (not counting FAME's annual $400,000 contribution).
As you will hear from various stakeholders, the participating medical schools and the bright, impressive students who have benefitted from it, this program has meant a great deal to Maine's medical community, Maine people (particularly those needing health care in rural, underserved areas,) and our promising youth who wish to live and work in our beautiful state to care for our people.
Finally, we fully recognize and are sensitive to the challenging budgetary
situation facing the Administration and this Legislature, but the conversation regarding the positive impact of this program, to both participating students and the communities they serve, as well as the ongoing sustainability of the program, is an important one to
have.
Thank you for your consideration of the bill. I will be happy to answer any questions you have.

March 31, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education,
I am writing to express my strong support for LD 581, "An Act to Fund the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program." As a lifelong Mainer and current medical student in the Maine Track Program, I have seen firsthand how scholarships like this help make medical education more accessible and allow students to train and stay in Maine.
I was born and raised in Scarborough, attended college in Maine, and chose to stay here for medical school. My decision to pursue a career in medicine was driven by my passion for both science and serving my community. The Maine Track Program has given me the opportunity to work and train in the place I call home, strengthening my connection to the people and healthcare system of Maine.
Scholarships like this help ease the financial burden of medical school, allowing students to focus on their education rather than the stress of overwhelming debt. In my case, the financial support I received made it possible for me to stay in Maine for a world-class medical education, rather than having to choose a more expensive private medical school out of state.
While my immediate future depends on the residency match process, my long-term goal is to return to Maine to practice medicine. This is my home, and both my partner and I want to build our lives and careers here.
Maintaining full funding for the Doctors for Maine's Future Scholarship Program is critical to ensuring that students who want to train and stay in Maine have the financial support necessary to do so. This program helps strengthen Maine's healthcare workforce at a time when it is needed most. I urge you to support LD 581 and continue investing in the future of healthcare in Maine.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Josh Passarelli
